To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
predator handling times can promote the coevolutionary stability of predator–prey populations through their influence on the spatial patterns of prey and predator patch preferences.

(1) coevolutionary interactions between predators and their prey promote the evolution of patch preferences in predator–preyer systems and that (2) long predator handling times stabilize predator–preyer interactions through their coevolutionary effects on patch preferences.

(i) predators with longer handling times are more likely to coevolve with prey that are aggregated in space and (ii) this coevolutionary outcome promotes the ecological stability of the predator–prey system.
